name: Jade Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a lettings negotiator at Harbour & Lane, a mid-size agency in the city centre, and I've been there just under two years. Most days I'm out showing flats from about ten, three or four viewings, then back at my desk chasing references, writing up listings and answering the inbox, which never stops. I like the tenants, honestly, especially the young couples who've been turned down five times and finally get a yes. What wears me out is landlords who want me to squeeze another hundred a month out of people who are already stretched.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you at work, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My manager Carol runs the branch, and I eat lunch most days with Priya, who does property management and knows every boiler in the city. I live with my partner Lewis, who drives the number 14 bus, in a rented one-bed above a launderette. We've got about three months of bills put by, which feels like a lot until the rent goes up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds a lot like what's already happening. We've got a tool that drafts listings and it's fine, but I still rewrite half of what it writes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. At work I'd joke with Priya that the listing writer still can't tell a damp patch from a shadow. Online I'd probably post that the real problem in lettings was never the paperwork, it was the rents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because my job's mostly safe in that picture. But the stuff that keeps me up doesn't change: our rent went up eight percent in March, and Lewis's shifts got cut over the summer. So it's not AI I'm worried about, it's the same squeeze as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and try to get better at it, because Carol says I'm still too slow on the paperwork. I'd use the listing tool for first drafts so I can fit in one more viewing a day. And I'd keep putting 200 a month aside, because three months of savings isn't a wall, it's a fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit tired. Like the future got cancelled and we're back to arguing about deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lewis's shifts were cut. If they're cut again, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We share an old Fiesta and it costs us about 150 a month with insurance, and I could do viewings on the tram if Carol let me book them closer together. After that it'd be eating out, which is already down to once a fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work you'd want to change in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the agency to stop charging tenants for things the law already says we can't, and to train juniors properly. I learned referencing from a laminated sheet Priya made. If AI isn't going to change anything, then let's at least fix the boring human stuff.

say: I'd joke that the **listing tool** still can't tell a damp patch from a shadow.
I'd post that the real problem in lettings was always **the rents**, not the paperwork.
think: My **job** looks mostly safe if AI stays a small helper.
The real worry is the **rent rise** and Lewis's cut shifts, which carry on regardless.
do: Use the **listing tool** for first drafts to fit in one more viewing a day.
Keep saving **200 a month**, and sell the shared car if Lewis's shifts drop again.
feel: **Relieved** about the job, but **tired** of the same money squeeze.
S0.quote: Three months of savings isn't a wall, it's a fence.
fieldNote: She separates AI worry from **money worry** quickly; rent is what she raises unprompted.
Her **progressive** streak shows in wanting tenant fees fixed rather than tech added.
She admits she's **slow on paperwork** and treats it as a skill gap, not a threat.

steps.text: Use the listing tool for first drafts to add a viewing a day
Put 200 a month into savings every payday
Sell the shared Fiesta if Lewis's bus shifts drop again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's closer to home. Half my day is exactly that list: booking, checking, answering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to make sure people aren't just let go, and that juniors get trained on the new systems, not replaced by them. I'd probably bring up joining a union, which nobody in our office has ever done. Online I'd share posts about protecting renters, because if software does the referencing, someone needs to check it isn't unfair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the first thing to go is the junior desk job, which is me. If the inbox answers itself and referencing is automatic, Carol needs two negotiators doing viewings, not four. And I'm not the best of the four, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd ask Carol to put me on the new system first, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd join the workers' union for property staff, which costs about 12 a month. And I'd push savings up from three months to five, even if that means no holiday next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in my stomach. Like waiting for a test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the best of the four. Who would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal, who started after me. He's lovely with tenants but can barely open a spreadsheet. And Priya, honestly, because a lot of property management is chasing contractors by email, and if the software books the plumber, what's left is the angry phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lewis that night, after hearing the news at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're fine for now but we're not booking the trip to his sister's wedding abroad. He'd say I'm panicking. I'd rather panic early with four months in the bank than late with one.

say: I'd say juniors should be **trained on new systems**, not replaced by them.
I'd raise **joining a union**, and share posts about checking automated tenant referencing for fairness.
think: The **junior desk job** is the first to go, and that's me.
If the inbox answers itself, the branch needs **two negotiators**, not four, and I'm not the strongest.
do: Ask Carol to put me on the **new system first** so I become the one who knows it.
Join the **property workers' union** for about 12 a month.
Build savings from three to **five months**, skipping next summer's holiday.
feel: **Anxious**, like waiting for a test result.
S1.quote: I'd rather panic early with four months in the bank than late with one.
fieldNote: She expects cuts to land on **juniors**, and is honest that she's weaker than colleagues.
Her instinct is **collective** first: the union, then personal training.
She worries for **Jamal and Priya**, whose days are mostly email and booking.

steps.text: Ask Carol for first training on the new lettings system
Join the property workers' union at about 12 a month
Skip next summer's holiday to reach five months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our tenancy even comes up for renewal twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say this needs governments to step in, fast, with income support and rules about firing people. I'd be at the march, if there is one. At work I'd say we should all stick together and not let the agency pick us off one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm gone by 2029. Valuations, listings, referencing, contracts, the inbox: all thinking work, all done by AI. The viewings stay human for a few years until the robots come, but nobody's paying an estate agent a full wage to unlock doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start training for something hands-on and people-heavy, maybe care work, because Lewis's mum gets carers and they're always short. I'd move us into a cheaper flat when the lease ends in June. And I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for a basic income, because I'd need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. And angry, because the people who own the AI will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before the robots mean for you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means about three years of door-opening work, maybe, at lower pay. I could do viewings part-time while I train. But I'd be one of a hundred agents all wanting the same few viewing shifts, so I don't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first, if both you and Lewis lost hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card, which has about 900 on it from the sofa. Rent comes first, always, because I've seen what happens to tenants who fall behind. I've written those letters myself.

say: I'd demand **income support** and rules on firing, and go to any march.
At work I'd urge colleagues to **stick together** so the agency can't pick us off.
think: The **thinking work** of lettings goes by 2029: listings, referencing, contracts and the inbox.
Viewings last a few more years, but **door-opening** won't pay a full wage.
do: Start training for **care work** this year, where carers are always short.
Move to a **cheaper flat** when the June lease ends.
Join a **basic income** campaign and rally colleagues to negotiate together.
feel: **Scared** for her income and **angry** at who profits.
S2.quote: Nobody's paying an estate agent a full wage to unlock doors.
fieldNote: She sees the **robot gap** as a few years of low-paid viewing shifts, not safety.
Her plan B is **care work**, drawn from watching Lewis's mum's carers.
Lettings makes her vivid about **arrears letters**; rent always gets paid first.

steps.text: Enrol on a care worker course this year
Move to a cheaper flat when the June lease ends
Join a campaign pushing for a basic income
Push colleagues to negotiate as a group with the agency

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32. That's enough time to do something, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and we should use it: retraining money, protections for renters and workers, all of it. I'd be telling the younger ones at work not to wait for the agency to look after them. Online I'd be the annoying one posting about union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think lettings as a junior job is done by then, but I'd have time to get out on my terms. The thinking work goes in 2031 and the viewings maybe in 2034. That's long enough to qualify in something where a person in the room matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time nursing access course next autumn, evenings, about two years, and stay at Harbour & Lane while I do it. We'd keep saving 200 a month and put off replacing the car. And I'd stay active in the union so there's a fight for decent redundancy pay when it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but more in control. Like I can see the cliff and I've got time to find the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, and not something else in property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because property is all screens and contracts underneath, and that's exactly what goes first. Nursing is hands and judgement and people at 3 a.m. Gloria, the nurse who visits Lewis's mum, told me they'll never have enough of them, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay at the agency while training. What if Carol cuts your hours before you're done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the cut and do bar shifts at the weekend. I did that at nineteen. It's not glamorous, but I'd rather pour pints than finish a course halfway.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and need retraining money and protections now.
I'd tell younger colleagues not to wait for **the agency** to look after them.
think: Junior lettings work is likely **finished by 2031**, but I can leave on my terms.
Five years is long enough to **qualify** where a person in the room matters.
do: Start an evening **nursing access course** next autumn while staying at the agency.
Keep saving **200 a month** and delay replacing the car.
Stay active in the **union** to fight for redundancy pay.
feel: **Nervous** but more **in control** than with two years.
S3.quote: Property is all screens and contracts underneath, and that's exactly what goes first.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn her **dread into a plan**, with a course and a start date.
She reasons that property is **screens underneath**, so she leaves the sector rather than adapting in it.
Her fallback is **bar shifts**, which she's done before.

steps.text: Start an evening nursing access course next autumn
Keep saving 200 a month and delay replacing the car
Stay active in the union to push for redundancy pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd be 37, maybe with kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if governments actually use it, and I'd be pushing for that. At work I'd say the agency should be paying for our training now, not in 2035. With friends I'd probably say I'm not worried, which is about half true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I can probably stay in lettings for a while and still get out. What worries me more is the kids question, because Lewis wants two and I'm not sure what jobs they'd even grow up into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency and get properly good at it for a few years, and take the lettings qualification Carol keeps mentioning. I'd start using the AI tools more so I'm not left behind. Around 2030 I'd move into training for something hands-on, probably nursing, and keep the union card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. More like a long to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell friends you're not worried, which is half true. What's the other half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other half is that ten years sounds long until you remember I've been renting for nine and still haven't saved a deposit. Plans slide. I've watched my own savings plan slide every time the rent goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the kids question change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might mean having them sooner, honestly, while Lewis and I both still have steady wages. That's a weird thing to decide because of AI. But you plan a family around money, and money is what this changes.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough if governments actually use it.
At work I'd argue the agency should **pay for training** now, not in 2035.
think: Ten years means I can **stay in lettings** a while and still get out.
The bigger question is **children**, and what work they'd grow up into.
do: Take the **lettings qualification** Carol keeps mentioning within the next year.
Use the **AI tools** more so I'm not left behind.
Plan to retrain for **hands-on work** around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frightened, like facing a long to-do list.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until you remember I've been renting for nine and still haven't saved a deposit.
fieldNote: With ten years she **leans in** to the current job before leaving it.
She is honest that **plans slide**, pointing at her own savings record.
AI unexpectedly reshapes **family timing**: she'd consider children sooner.

steps.text: Take the lettings qualification Carol keeps recommending
Use the agency's AI tools for listings and inbox replies
Talk with Lewis about having children sooner on two wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to train for anything before the rent's due. What would help is money while you retrain, real money, not a voucher for an online course. And rules that stop agencies sacking juniors first just because we're cheapest to get rid of.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about tenants. If agencies run on AI, the people renting flats lose the one human who might bend a rule for them. I've let a family pay a deposit in two parts because the dad had just changed jobs, and no software would have done that.

headlineQuote: I've let a family pay a deposit in two parts because the dad had just changed jobs, and no software would have done that.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old lettings negotiator** at a city agency, renting a one-bed with Lewis, a bus driver.
She leans **progressive**, sides with tenants and reaches first for a **union** when work looks threatened.
She sees her **desk tasks** as the first to go and admits she's weaker than colleagues.
With two years she'd retrain for **care work**; with five or ten she plans a **nursing course**.
Her steady worry, AI or not, is **rent** and a savings cushion that never seems to grow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to retrain before the **rent** is due.
whatWouldHelp: **Real income** while retraining, not a voucher for an online course.
Rules that stop agencies **sacking juniors first** because they're cheapest to let go.
